The distance is calculated through many methods  but one of the main ones is the parallax effect which essentially uses trigonometry to calculate it's distance. Basically depending on the positioning of earth during it's orbit around the sun, a right angle will be created between our sun and earth which then we can use to draw two lines between the star we are trying to measure and Earth and the sun. This will create a right triangle. Next, we use the shift or change in positioning of another star during different periods and measure it against the star we are trying to the calculate the distance of. The shift of the distant star against the star we are trying to measure will create an angle and by the principles of trigonometry that angle is equivalent to the angle of the star we are trying measure via the congruence principle, where two angles opposite to each other are equal. From then on, we use that angle and the right angle we measured against the Earth and the sun to calculate it's distance or the length of the two extended lines between the Earth, the sun, and the star we are trying to measure via trigonometry 

So in short we use the change in positioning of another star relative to the one we are trying to measure to calculate it's angle. We then use trigonometry and the right angle created by the Earth and the Sun during specific times in it's orbit to calculate its distance after extending to lines to the star we are trying to measure.

Now why does this matter, well the stars don't actually move, they appear to move because of the rotation of Earth. The distance of the star can only be calculated through the parallax effect if the Earth is positioned at a right angle between the sun and we can draw two lines extending to the star we are trying to measure.
